sentences.zh: 顏延之字延年，琅邪臨沂人也。

translations.literal: Yan Yanzhi, styled Yannian, was a man of Langya, Linyi.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Yanzhi, whose style was Yannian, came from Langya commandery, Linyi county.

sentences.zh: 曾祖含，右光祿大夫。

translations.literal: His great-grandfather Han was Right Director of the Imperial Household.
translations.idiomatic: His great-grandfather Yan Han served as Right Director of the Imperial Household.

sentences.zh: 祖約，零陵太守。

translations.literal: His grandfather Yue was Administrator of Lingling.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Yan Yue was Administrator of Lingling.

sentences.zh: 父顯，護軍司馬。

translations.literal: His father Xian was Marshal of the Protector-General.
translations.idiomatic: His father Yan Xian held the post of Marshal under the Protector-General.

sentences.zh: 延之少孤貧，居負郭，室巷甚陋。

translations.literal: Yanzhi was orphaned young and poor; he lived outside the city wall, and his lane and rooms were very shabby.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi lost his father early and grew up poor, dwelling just beyond the city wall in a mean lane and hovel.

sentences.zh: 好讀書，無所不覽，文章之美，冠絕當時。

translations.literal: He loved reading and browsed everything; the beauty of his writings surpassed all of his time.
translations.idiomatic: He loved books and read widely; the excellence of his prose stood above everyone of his day.

sentences.zh: 飲酒不護細行，年三十，猶未婚。

translations.literal: He drank wine and did not guard minor conduct; at thirty he still was unmarried.
translations.idiomatic: He drank heavily and paid little heed to propriety; at thirty he was still unmarried.

sentences.zh: 妹適東莞劉憲之，穆之子也。

translations.literal: His younger sister married Liu Xianzhi of Dongguan, son of Muzi.
translations.idiomatic: His younger sister had married Liu Xianzhi of Dongguan, a son of Liu Muzhi.

sentences.zh: 穆之既與延之通家，又聞其美，將仕之，先欲相見，延之不往也。

translations.literal: Muzhi was already connected to Yanzhi's family by marriage and had heard of his excellence; he wished to employ him and first wanted to meet him, but Yanzhi would not go.
translations.idiomatic: Muzhi was already related to Yanzhi by marriage and, hearing of his talent, meant to take him into service and wished to meet him first; Yanzhi refused to call on him.

sentences.zh: 後將軍、吳國內史劉柳以為行參軍，因轉主簿，豫章公世子中軍行參軍。

translations.literal: General of the Rear and Domestic Administrator of Wu Liu Liu made him Acting Retainer; he was then transferred to Chief Clerk, and Acting Retainer in the Heir Apparent's Central Army of the Duke of Yuzhang.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Liu, General of the Rear and Domestic Administrator of Wu, appointed him Acting Retainer; he was later made Chief Clerk, then Acting Retainer in the Central Army of the Duke of Yuzhang's heir.

sentences.zh: 義熙十二年，高祖北伐，有宋公之授，府遣一使慶殊命，參起居，延之與同府王參軍俱奉使至洛陽，道中作詩二首，文辭藻麗，為謝晦、傅亮所賞。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year of Yixi, the Founder marched north; upon receiving investiture as Duke of Song, the office sent an envoy to celebrate the extraordinary appointment and attend to imperial audiences. Yanzhi and Wang, a staff retainer from the same office, were both sent as envoys to Luoyang. On the road they composed two poems; the language was ornate and splendid, and Xie Hui and Fu Liang admired them.
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth year of Yixi (416), when the Founder Liu Yu campaigned north and received the title Duke of Song, the staff sent an envoy to mark the exceptional honor and attend court. Yanzhi and a fellow retainer named Wang went together to Luoyang; en route they wrote two poems whose diction was rich and polished, winning the praise of Xie Hui and Fu Liang.

sentences.zh: 宋國建，奉常鄭鮮之舉為博士，仍遷世子舍人。

translations.literal: When the State of Song was established, Director of Ceremonies Zheng Xianzhi recommended him as Erudite; he was then moved to Attendant of the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: After the Song state was founded, Zheng Xianzhi, Director of Ceremonies, recommended him as Erudite, and he was soon transferred to Attendant of the Heir Apparent.

sentences.zh: 高祖受命，補太子舍人。

translations.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate, he was appointed Attendant of the Crown Prince.
translations.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Yanzhi was appointed Attendant of the Crown Prince.

sentences.zh: 雁門人周續之隱居廬山，儒學著稱，永初中，徵詣京師，開館以居之。

translations.literal: Zhou Xuanshi of Yanmen lived in seclusion on Mount Lu and was renowned in Confucian learning; in the early Yongchu era he was summoned to the capital, and a hall was opened for him to dwell in.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Xuanshi of Yanmen, a celebrated Confucian recluse on Mount Lu, was summoned to the capital in early Yongchu (424–424) and given a lecture hall to live in.

sentences.zh: 高祖親幸，朝彥畢至，延之官列猶卑，引升上席。

translations.literal: The Founder visited in person; court worthies all arrived. Yanzhi's official rank was still low, yet he was led up to the upper seat.
translations.idiomatic: The Founder came in person; the leading men of court were all present. Though Yanzhi still held a humble rank, he was brought to the seat of honor.

sentences.zh: 上使問續之三義，續之雅仗辭辯，延之每折以簡要。

translations.literal: The emperor had him question Xuanshi on the Three Meanings; Xuanshi relied on his eloquence, and Yanzhi each time refuted him with brevity and precision.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor set him to examine Xuanshi on the Three Meanings. Xuanshi leaned on his eloquence, but Yanzhi repeatedly cut him down with terse, pointed replies.

sentences.zh: 既連挫續之，上又使還自敷釋，言約理暢，莫不稱善。

translations.literal: Having repeatedly defeated Xuanshi, the emperor also had him return and expound on his own; his words were concise and the reasoning clear, and none failed to praise him.
translations.idiomatic: After he had repeatedly bested Xuanshi, the emperor had him explain his own views as well; his speech was spare yet lucid, and everyone praised him.

sentences.zh: 徙尚書儀曹郎，太子中舍人。

translations.literal: He was moved to Gentleman of the Ministry of Rites, and Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Crown Prince.
translations.idiomatic: He was transferred to Gentleman of the Ministry of Rites and Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Crown Prince.

sentences.zh: 時尚書令傅亮自以文義之美，一時莫及，延之負其才辭，不為之下，亮甚疾焉。

translations.literal: At that time Minister of Works Fu Liang considered the beauty of his literary meaning unmatched in the age; Yanzhi, relying on his talent in letters, would not place himself below him, and Liang greatly resented this.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Liang, then Minister of Works, believed no one of the time could rival him in literary brilliance; Yanzhi, confident in his own gifts, refused to yield, and Liang came to detest him.

sentences.zh: 廬陵王義真頗好辭義，待接甚厚，徐羨之等疑延之為同異，意甚不悅。

translations.literal: Prince of Luling Yizhen was quite fond of literary meaning and treated him with great warmth; Xu Xianzhi and others suspected Yanzhi of being of a different faction and were very displeased.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Yizhen of Luling was fond of letters and treated Yanzhi generously; Xu Xianzhi and his circle suspected Yanzhi of siding against them and were deeply displeased.

sentences.zh: 少帝即位，以為正員郎，兼中書，尋徙員外常侍，出為始安太守。

translations.literal: When the Young Emperor acceded, he was made Regular Gentleman and concurrently Secretary; soon he was moved to Supernumerary Regular Attendant and sent out as Administrator of Shi'an.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Shao came to the throne, Yanzhi was made Regular Gentleman with concurrent duties in the Secretariat; he was soon transferred to Supernumerary Regular Attendant and sent out as Administrator of Shi'an.

sentences.zh: 領軍將軍謝晦謂延之曰：「昔荀勗忌阮咸，斥為始平郡，今卿又為始安，可謂二始。」

translations.literal: General-in-Chief Xie Hui said to Yanzhi: "In the past Xun Xu resented Ruan Xian and banished him to Shiping commandery; now you are again made Administrator of Shi'an—this may be called the two Shi's."
translations.idiomatic: Xie Hui, General-in-Chief, told him: "Long ago Xun Xu envied Ruan Xian and sent him off to Shiping; now you are posted to Shi'an—you might call it a pair of 'Shi' banishments."

sentences.zh: 黃門郎殷景仁亦謂之曰：「所謂俗惡俊異，世疵文雅。」

translations.literal: Gentleman at the Yellow Gate Yin Jingren also said to him: "What is called the vulgar hating the outstanding, the age faulting refinement."
translations.idiomatic: Yin Jingren, Gentleman at the Yellow Gate, added: "As the saying goes, the coarse hate the exceptional, and the age finds fault with elegance."

sentences.zh: 延之之郡，道經汨潭，為湘州刺史張邵祭屈原文以致其意，曰：

translations.literal: When Yanzhi went to his commandery, his route passed the Mi Pool; for Xiangzhou Inspector Zhang Shao he offered a sacrifice to Qu Yuan's text to convey his intent, saying:
translations.idiomatic: On his way to take up the post, Yanzhi passed the Mi Pool and, at the request of Zhang Shao, Inspector of Xiangzhou, composed a sacrificial text to Qu Yuan to express his feelings. It reads:

sentences.zh: :恭承帝命，建旟舊楚。

translations.literal: Respectfully receiving the emperor's command, I raise the banner in old Chu.
translations.idiomatic: Reverently bearing the imperial charge, I raise my standard in ancient Chu.

sentences.zh: 訪懷沙之淵，得捐佩之浦。

translations.literal: I visit the deep of Embracing Sand, and reach the shore of Casting Aside the Girdle-Pendant.
translations.idiomatic: I come to the depths where he embraced the sand, and to the bank where he cast off his jade pendant.

sentences.zh: 弭節羅潭，艤舟汨渚，敬祭楚三閭大夫屈君之靈：

translations.literal: I halt my carriage at the Luo Pool, moor my boat at the Mi Ford, and reverently sacrifice to the spirit of Lord Qu, Three-Minister Grandee of Chu:
translations.idiomatic: I rein in at the Luo Pool and moor at the Mi Ford, reverently offering sacrifice to the spirit of Lord Qu, Three-Minister Grandee of Chu:

sentences.zh: :蘭薰而摧，玉貞則折。

translations.literal: Orchids fragrant yet are broken down; jade firm yet is snapped.
translations.idiomatic: Orchids may perfume the air yet still be uprooted; jade may be hard yet still be shattered.

sentences.zh: 物忌堅芳，人諱明潔。

translations.literal: Things resent firm fragrance; men shun bright purity.
translations.idiomatic: The world begrudges what is firm and fragrant; men fear what is bright and clean.

sentences.zh: 曰若先生，逢辰之缺。

translations.literal: Alas, good sir, you met a flawed age.
translations.idiomatic: Alas, good master—you were born into a broken time.

sentences.zh: 溫風迨時，飛霜急節。

translations.literal: Warm winds come at their season; flying frost hastens the nodes.
translations.idiomatic: Warm breezes arrive in season, yet flying frost hurries the turning year.

sentences.zh: 嬴、芊遘紛，昭、懷不端。

translations.literal: Ying and Qian encountered turmoil; Zhao and Huai were not upright.
translations.idiomatic: Under Kings Ying and Qian strife arose; Kings Zhao and Huai lost their way.

sentences.zh: 謀折儀、尚，貞蔑椒、蘭。

translations.literal: Plots broke Yi and Shang; steadfastness scorned Jiao and Lan.
translations.idiomatic: Intrigue broke down Shang Yi; loyalty was mocked, and Jiao and Lan despised.

sentences.zh: 身絕郢闕，迹遍湘干。

translations.literal: His person was cut off from the Ying gate-towers; his traces spread along the Xiang banks.
translations.idiomatic: His body was severed from the towers of Ying; his footsteps ranged the shores of the Xiang.

sentences.zh: 比物荃蓀，連類龍鸞。

translations.literal: He likened things to sweet-flag and asarum, and linked kinds to dragon and phoenix.
translations.idiomatic: He matched things to iris and wild ginger, pairing kinds with dragon and phoenix.

sentences.zh: 聲溢金石，志華日月。

translations.literal: His voice overflowed metal and stone; his will outshone sun and moon.
translations.idiomatic: His voice rang beyond bronze and stone; his purpose outshone sun and moon.

sentences.zh: 如彼樹芬，實穎實發。

translations.literal: Like that fragrant tree, its ears full, its blossoms opening.
translations.idiomatic: Like a fragrant tree in full ear and bloom.

sentences.zh: 望汨心欷，瞻羅思越。

translations.literal: Gazing on the Mi, the heart sighs; looking on the Luo, thoughts leap beyond.
translations.idiomatic: Gazing on the Mi, the heart sighs; looking toward the Luo, thought flies beyond.

sentences.zh: 藉用可塵，昭忠難闕。

translations.literal: By this offering dust may be swept; to display loyalty none may omit.
translations.idiomatic: With this humble offering we may brush away dust; to proclaim loyalty nothing may be left undone.

sentences.zh: 元嘉三年，羨之等誅，徵為中書侍郎，尋轉太子中庶子，頃之，領步兵校尉，賞遇甚厚。

translations.literal: In the third year of Yuanjia, Xu Xianzhi and others were executed; he was summoned as Vice Director of the Secretariat, soon transferred to Vice Grandee of the Crown Prince's Household, and shortly after concurrently Colonel of Footsoldiers, with very generous rewards and favor.
translations.idiomatic: In the third year of Yuanjia (426), after Xu Xianzhi and his faction were put to death, Yanzhi was recalled as Vice Director of the Secretariat, then made Vice Grandee of the Crown Prince's Household; soon he also served as Colonel of Footsoldiers and enjoyed lavish favor.

sentences.zh: 延之好酒疎誕，不能斟酌當世，見劉湛、殷景仁專當要任，意有不平，常云：「天下之務，當與天下共之，豈一人之智所能獨了！」

translations.literal: Yanzhi loved wine and was unrestrained and eccentric; he could not measure the present age. Seeing Liu Zhan and Yin Jingren monopolize key posts, he was discontent and often said: "The affairs of the realm ought to be shared with the realm—how can one man's wisdom finish them alone!"
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi drank heavily and was blunt and eccentric, ill suited to court the times. Seeing Liu Zhan and Yin Jingren monopolize power, he grew resentful and would say, "The empire's business should be the empire's business—can one man's wit settle it all?"

sentences.zh: 辭甚激揚，每犯權要。

translations.literal: His words were very heated and exalted, and he often offended the powerful.
translations.idiomatic: His language was fierce, and he repeatedly gave offense to men in power.

sentences.zh: 謂湛曰：「吾名器不升，當由作卿家吏。」

translations.literal: He said to Zhan: "My name and office do not rise—it must be because I served as your family's clerk."
translations.idiomatic: He told Liu Zhan, "My rank never rises—no doubt because I once served as a clerk in your household."

sentences.zh: 湛深恨焉，言於彭城王義康，出為永嘉太守。

translations.literal: Zhan deeply hated this and spoke to Prince of Pengcheng Yikang; he was sent out as Administrator of Yongjia.
translations.idiomatic: Zhan hated this deeply and spoke to Prince Yikang of Pengcheng; Yanzhi was sent out as Administrator of Yongjia.

sentences.zh: 延之甚怨憤，乃作五君詠以述竹林七賢，山濤、王戎以貴顯被黜，詠嵇康曰：「鸞翮有時鎩，龍性誰能馴。」

translations.literal: Yanzhi was very resentful and angry, and composed Odes to the Five Lords to treat the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove; Shan Tao and Wang Rong were omitted for their noble prominence. On Ji Kang he wrote: "The phoenix pinion is sometimes clipped; who can tame a dragon's nature?"
translations.idiomatic: Burning with resentment, Yanzhi wrote his Odes to the Five Lords about the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, leaving out Shan Tao and Wang Rong as men who had risen to wealth and rank. Of Ji Kang he wrote: "A phoenix wing may be clipped in its season—who can tame a dragon's nature?"

sentences.zh: 詠阮籍曰：「物故可不論，塗窮能無慟。」

translations.literal: On Ruan Ji: "When things are past one need not discuss them; when the road ends how can one not grieve?"
translations.idiomatic: Of Ruan Ji: "When things are done with, why argue? When the road runs out, who does not mourn?"

sentences.zh: 詠阮咸曰：「屢薦不入官，一麾乃出守。」

translations.literal: On Ruan Xian: "Repeatedly recommended yet not entering office; one wave of the hand and he is sent out to govern."
translations.idiomatic: Of Ruan Xian: "Recommended again and again, yet never given office—a single gesture, and he is sent to rule a province."

sentences.zh: 詠劉伶曰：「韜精日沉飲，誰知非荒宴。」

translations.literal: On Liu Ling: "Hiding his essence, daily drowning in drink—who knows it is not a wild feast?"
translations.idiomatic: Of Liu Ling: "Hoarding his spirit, he sinks daily into wine—who knows it is not a feast of despair?"

sentences.zh: 此四句，蓋自序也。

translations.literal: These four lines were plainly his own self-account.
translations.idiomatic: These four lines were plainly his own self-portrait.

sentences.zh: 湛及義康以其辭旨不遜，大怒。

translations.literal: Zhan and Yikang, because his words and intent were not deferential, were greatly enraged.
translations.idiomatic: Zhan and Yikang, taking his verses as insolent, were furious.

sentences.zh: 時延之已拜，欲黜為遠郡，太祖與義康詔曰：「降延之為小邦不政，有謂其在都邑，豈動物情，罪過彰著，亦士庶共悉，直欲選代，令思愆里閭。

translations.literal: At that time Yanzhi had already received appointment; they wished to demote him to a distant commandery. The Founder instructed Yikang: "Demoting Yanzhi to a small state is not for poor governance—some say that in the capital he stirs men's feelings; his faults are conspicuous and known to gentlemen and commoners alike. We simply wish to choose a replacement and let him reflect on his errors in his home lane.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi had already accepted the post, but they meant to banish him to a remote commandery. The Founder wrote to Yikang: "Sending Yanzhi to a minor post is not because he governs badly. Some say that in the capital he stirs people's hearts; his faults are plain and known to all. We only want to replace him and let him repent at home.

sentences.zh: 猶復不悛，當驅往東土。

translations.literal: If he still does not reform, he should be driven to the eastern lands.
translations.idiomatic: If he still will not mend his ways, drive him to the eastern marches.

sentences.zh: 乃志難恕，自可隨事錄治。

translations.literal: If his will is hard to forgive, he may naturally be dealt with according to the matter on record.
translations.idiomatic: If his intent is unforgivable, punish him as the case warrants.

sentences.zh: 殷、劉意咸無異也。」

translations.literal: Yin and Liu's intentions were all the same."
translations.idiomatic: Yin and Liu were of the same mind."

sentences.zh: 乃以光祿勳車仲遠代之。

translations.literal: Director of the Imperial Household Che Zhongyuan was made to replace him.
translations.idiomatic: Che Zhongyuan, Director of the Imperial Household, was appointed in his stead.

sentences.zh: 延之與仲遠世素不協，屏居里巷，不豫人間者七載。

translations.literal: Yanzhi and Zhongyuan had long been at odds by family tradition; he withdrew to his lane and did not take part in worldly affairs for seven years.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi and the Che family had long been at odds; he shut himself in his lane and kept out of public life for seven years.

sentences.zh: 中書令王球名公子，遺務事外，延之慕焉，球亦愛其材，情好甚款。

translations.literal: Director of the Secretariat Wang Qiu was a famous nobleman's son who left affairs behind and dwelt apart; Yanzhi admired him, and Qiu also loved his talent—their affection was very warm.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Qiu, Director of the Secretariat, was a celebrated nobleman's son who shunned office and lived apart; Yanzhi admired him, and Qiu in turn prized his talent—they became close friends.

sentences.zh: 延之居常罄匱，球輒贍之。

translations.literal: Yanzhi in his dwelling was often utterly destitute; Qiu would always supply him.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhi was often penniless at home; Qiu regularly supported him.

sentences.zh: 晉恭思皇后葬，應須百官，湛之取義熙元年除身，以延之兼侍中。

translations.literal: At the burial of Empress Gongsi of Jin, all officials were required; Zhan took the appointment document of the first year of Yixi and made Yanzhi concurrent Attendant-in-Ordinary.
translations.idiomatic: For the burial of Empress Gongsi of Jin, all officials were required to attend. Zhan dug up Yanzhi's appointment record from the first year of Yixi (405) and made him concurrent Attendant-in-Ordinary.

sentences.zh: 邑吏送札，延之醉，投札於地曰：「顏延之未能事生，焉能事死！」

translations.literal: The district clerk delivered the summons; Yanzhi was drunk and threw the summons to the ground, saying: "Yan Yanzhi could not serve the living—how could he serve the dead!"
translations.idiomatic: When the district clerk brought the summons, Yanzhi, drunk, flung it to the ground and said, "Yan Yanzhi could not serve the living—how should he serve the dead?"

sentences.zh: 閑居無事，為庭誥之文。

translations.literal: Living in retirement without affairs, he composed a text of Household Admonitions.
translations.idiomatic: In his leisure at home he wrote his Household Admonitions.

sentences.zh: 今刪其繁辭，存其正，著于篇。

translations.literal: Now its redundant language is cut away and the essential kept, set down in this chapter.
translations.idiomatic: Here the redundant passages are cut away and the essential passages retained for this chapter.

sentences.zh: 曰：

translations.literal: It says:
translations.idiomatic: It reads:

sentences.zh: :庭誥者，施於閨庭之內，謂不遠也。

translations.literal: Household Admonitions are applied within the inner court—meaning what is not far off.
translations.idiomatic: Household Admonitions are meant for the inner court—for what lies close at hand.

sentences.zh: 吾年居秋方，慮先草木，故遽以未聞，誥爾在庭。

translations.literal: My years stand in the autumn quarter; I fear to go before grass and trees, and therefore hasten, while you have not yet heard, to admonish you who are in the court.
translations.idiomatic: My years stand in autumn's quarter; I fear I may wither before the grasses and trees, and so I hasten, while you are still unawares, to admonish you who are in the household.

sentences.zh: 若立履之方，規鑒之明，已列通人之規，不復續論。

translations.literal: As for the methods of establishing conduct and the clarity of rules and mirrors, these are already set out in the standards of accomplished men and are not discussed further here.
translations.idiomatic: The ways of upright conduct and the standards of judgment are already laid down by wise men of old and need not be repeated here.

sentences.zh: 今所載咸其素蓄，本乎性靈，而致之心用。

translations.literal: What is recorded here is all his long-stored views, rooted in native spirit and brought to bear on the mind's employment.
translations.idiomatic: What follows is drawn from his lifelong convictions, rooted in his nature and meant for practical use of the mind.

sentences.zh: 夫選言務一，不尚煩密，而至於備議者，蓋以網諸情非。

translations.literal: In choosing words one aims at unity and does not esteem prolix detail; yet when discussion is made complete, it is in order to net the many ways feeling goes astray.
translations.idiomatic: In choosing words one seeks unity, not prolix detail; yet when the discussion is full, it is to cast a net over every way feeling can go wrong.

sentences.zh: 古語曰得鳥者羅之一目，而一目之羅，無時得鳥矣。

translations.literal: An old saying runs: he who gets birds has a net of many meshes, but a net of one mesh never gets birds.
translations.idiomatic: As the old saying goes, the hunter who catches birds uses a net of many meshes; a net with but one mesh never catches a bird.

sentences.zh: 此其積意之方。

translations.literal: This is the method of accumulating intent.
translations.idiomatic: That is the method of gathering one's purpose.

sentences.zh: :道者識之公，情者德之私。

translations.literal: The Way is the public side of understanding; feeling is the private side of virtue.
translations.idiomatic: The Way is what understanding holds in common; feeling is what virtue keeps private.

sentences.zh: 公通，可以使神明加嚮；

translations.literal: What is public and penetrating can make the spirits incline toward one;
translations.idiomatic: What is open and shared can draw the spirits to incline toward you;

sentences.zh: 私塞，不能令妻子移心。

translations.literal: what is private and blocked cannot make even wife and children shift their hearts.
translations.idiomatic: what is private and closed cannot even move wife and children to change their hearts.

sentences.zh: 是以昔之善為士者，必捐情反道，合公屏私。

translations.literal: Therefore those of old who were good at being gentlemen always cast off feeling and returned to the Way, joining the public and screening out the private.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the gentlemen of old always set feeling aside and returned to the Way, embracing what is public and shutting out what is private.

sentences.zh: :尋尺之身，而以天地為心；

translations.literal: A body of a few feet, yet taking heaven and earth as one's heart;
translations.idiomatic: Though one's body spans only a few feet, let heaven and earth be one's heart;

sentences.zh: 數紀之壽，常以金石為量。

translations.literal: a life of several reckonings of years, yet constantly taking metal and stone as one's measure.
translations.idiomatic: though one's life lasts only a few dozen years, let metal and stone be one's measure.

sentences.zh: 觀夫古先垂戒，長老餘論，雖用細制，每以不朽見銘；

translations.literal: Observing how the ancients left warnings and elders left remaining discussions—though they used minute regulations, they were each inscribed with a view to imperishability;
translations.idiomatic: Consider how the ancients left warnings and elders left counsel: though they spoke of small rules, they inscribed them to endure;

sentences.zh: 繕築末迹，咸以可久承志。

translations.literal: repairing and building trifling traces, all with the aim that intent might be carried on for long.
translations.idiomatic: even in repairing trivial things, they aimed to pass their purpose down for long.

sentences.zh: 況樹德立義，收族長家，而不思經遠乎。

translations.literal: How much more when planting virtue and establishing righteousness, gathering the clan and extending the family—will one not think of lasting far?
translations.idiomatic: How much more when planting virtue, establishing righteousness, gathering the clan, and building the household—will you not think of what endures?

sentences.zh: :曰身行不足遺之後人。

translations.literal: It is said: personal conduct alone is not enough to bequeath to later men.
translations.idiomatic: As the saying goes, conduct alone is not enough to leave to posterity.

sentences.zh: 欲求子孝必先慈，將責弟悌務為友。

translations.literal: If you wish sons to be filial, you must first be kind; if you will demand younger brothers' fraternal duty, you must yourself be friendly.
translations.idiomatic: If you want filial sons, be kind first; if you expect fraternal duty from younger brothers, be a friend to them yourself.

sentences.zh: 雖孝不待慈，而慈固植孝；

translations.literal: Though filial piety does not wait upon kindness, kindness firmly plants filial piety;
translations.idiomatic: Filial piety does not depend on kindness, yet kindness surely plants filial piety;

sentences.zh: 悌非期友，而友亦立悌。

translations.literal: fraternal duty is not awaited from friendship, yet friendship also establishes fraternal duty.
translations.idiomatic: fraternal duty is not won by demanding friendship, yet friendship also establishes it.

sentences.zh: :夫和之不備，或應以不和；

translations.literal: When harmony is not complete, one may respond with disharmony;
translations.idiomatic: When harmony is incomplete, one may answer with discord;

sentences.zh: 猶信不足焉，必有不信。

translations.literal: just as when trust is insufficient, there must be distrust.
translations.idiomatic: just as where trust falls short, distrust must follow.

sentences.zh: 儻知恩意相生，情理相出，可使家有參、柴，人皆由、損。

translations.literal: If one only knew that favor and intent give birth to each other and principle and feeling emerge from each other, one could make the family have Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be Yan Hui or Min Sun.
translations.idiomatic: If you grasp that kindness and intent breed one another and that principle and feeling arise together, your household may hold men like Zeng Shen and Gao Chai, and every man be a Yan Hui or Min Sun.

sentences.zh: :夫內居德本，外夷民譽，言高一世，處之逾默，器重一時，體之滋沖，不以所能干眾，不以所長議物，淵泰入道，與天為人者，士之上也。

translations.literal: One who inwardly dwells in the root of virtue and outwardly levels popular praise; whose words tower over an age yet in bearing grows ever more silent; whose weight of talent fills a time yet whose substance grows ever more yielding; who does not use his abilities to press upon the multitude nor use his strengths to judge things; who is deep, peaceful, and enters the Way, making himself a counterpart to Heaven—such a man is the highest grade of gentleman.
translations.idiomatic: The highest gentleman keeps virtue at his core and sets popular praise aside; his words may tower over an age, yet he grows quieter in manner; his talent may weigh on a generation, yet his substance grows more yielding. He does not thrust his abilities upon the crowd or judge things by his strengths alone. Deep, serene, and entered into the Way, he stands as heaven's counterpart among men.

sentences.zh: 若不能遺聲，欲人出己，知柄在虛求，不可校得，敬慕謙通，畏避矜踞，思廣監擇，從其遠猷，文理精出，而言稱未達，論問宣茂，而不以居身，此其亞也。

translations.literal: If one cannot leave behind reputation yet wishes others to yield place to oneself, knowing that the handle lies in empty seeking and cannot be matched and obtained; who reveres and admires modest passage, fears and avoids arrogant sitting; who thinks to broaden observation and selection and follow far-reaching plans; whose pattern and principle are finely brought forth yet whose words claim they have not arrived; whose discourse and questioning are broadly displayed yet not made the substance of the person—this is the next grade.
translations.idiomatic: The next grade cannot shed reputation yet wants others to yield to him, knowing that standing is won by empty striving, not by contest. He reveres humility, shuns arrogance, seeks wide counsel, and follows far-reaching plans. His writing is refined, yet he claims he has not arrived; his discourse is rich, yet he does not make it his whole self.

sentences.zh: 若乃聞實之為貴，以辯畫所克，見聲之取榮，謂爭奪可獲，言不出於戶牖，自以為道義久立，才未信於僕妾，而曰我有以過人，於是感苟銳之志，馳傾觖之望，豈悟已挂有識之裁，入修家之誡乎。

translations.literal: As for one who hears that substance is prized and relies on disputation and scheming to overcome; who sees that reputation wins glory and thinks struggle and seizure can obtain it; whose words do not go beyond door and window yet who thinks righteousness long established; whose talent is not trusted even by servant girls yet who says he has what surpasses others—thereupon stirred by reckless sharp ambition, he gallops off after perverse and resentful hopes. Does he realize he has already hung on the judgment of those with understanding and entered the admonitions for cultivating the family?
translations.idiomatic: Lower still is the man who prizes substance only in rumor, who wins by argument and intrigue, who thinks glory comes from quarreling and seizing, whose speech never leaves his door yet who believes his righteousness long established, whose talent is not trusted even by maidservants yet who claims to surpass others—then, stirred by reckless ambition, he chases twisted resentments. Does he see that the wise already judge him and that he has fallen under the household's admonitions?

sentences.zh: 記所云「千人所指，無病自死」者也。

translations.literal: This is what the Record means by "When a thousand men point at one, without illness he dies of himself."
translations.idiomatic: This is what the Record means: "When a thousand men point at you, you die though no illness touches you."

sentences.zh: 行近於此者，吾不願聞之矣。

translations.literal: Conduct approaching this—I do not wish to hear of it.
translations.idiomatic: Conduct that approaches this—I do not wish to hear of it in my house.

sentences.zh: :凡有知能，預有文論，若不練之庶士，校之羣言，通才所歸，前流所與，焉得以成名乎。

translations.literal: All who have knowledge and ability and beforehand possess literary discourse—if they do not temper themselves among ordinary gentlemen and test themselves against the many words, the convergences to which accomplished talent goes and the gifts the former stream bestows—how can they thereby obtain a name?
translations.idiomatic: Whoever has talent and presumes to discourse on letters, if he does not hone himself among ordinary scholars and test his words against the wider world—the paths great talent takes and the gifts the masters left—how will he make a name?

sentences.zh: 若呻吟於牆室之內，喧囂於黨輩之間，竊議以迷寡聞，妲語以敵要說，是短算所出，而非長見所上。

translations.literal: If one moans within walled rooms and clamors among factional peers, using stolen discussion to bewilder scant hearing and shallow words to match essential discourse—this is the product of short reckoning, not what long vision mounts to.
translations.idiomatic: If you moan within your walls and shout among your clique, using stolen gossip to bewilder the narrow-minded and shallow chatter to match serious discourse, that is the fruit of short thinking, not of far sight.

sentences.zh: 適值尊朋臨座，稠覽博論，而言不入於高聽，人見棄於眾視，則慌若迷塗失偶，黶如深夜撤燭，銜聲茹氣，腆默而歸，豈識向之夸慢，祇足以成今之沮喪邪。

translations.literal: Just when honored friends take their seats and dense reading and broad discussion unfold, if one's words do not enter lofty hearing and one is seen cast off by the multitude's gaze, then one is flustered as if lost on a road without a mate, dark as if in deep night when candles are withdrawn—holding voice, swallowing breath, returning in shameful silence. Does one recognize that former boastful arrogance was only enough to make present dejection?
translations.idiomatic: When honored friends are seated and debate runs wide, if your words fail to reach discerning ears and the company turns away, you will be flustered as one lost on the road without a companion, benighted as when candles are snuffed at midnight—clamping your voice, swallowing your breath, slinking home in shame. Do you see that yesterday's boasting only breeds today's defeat?

sentences.zh: 此固少壯之廢，爾其戒之。

translations.literal: This is indeed the ruin of youth and prime—take warning from it.
translations.idiomatic: This is the ruin of the young and strong—take it as your warning.

sentences.zh: :夫以怨誹為心者，未有達無心救得喪，多見誚耳。

translations.literal: Those who take resentment and slander as their heart—none have reached attainment. Without heart one cannot rescue gain and loss; one mostly meets ridicule.
translations.idiomatic: Those who make resentment and slander their heart never attain anything. Without detachment you cannot master fortune and loss—you will mostly meet ridicule.

sentences.zh: 此蓋臧獲之為，豈識量之為事哉。

translations.literal: This is roughly the conduct of menials—how is it the affair of those who know measure?
translations.idiomatic: That is the way of servants—how is it the business of men who know their measure?

sentences.zh: 是以德聲令氣，愈上每高，忿言懟議，每下愈發，有尚於君子者，寧可不務勉邪。

translations.literal: Therefore virtuous reputation and fine spirit—the higher they go, the higher each step; angry words and contentious debate—the lower they go, the more they break out. For one who aspires to be a gentleman, can he not strive to exert himself?
translations.idiomatic: Thus good repute and noble spirit rise higher with every step, while angry words and quarrels sink lower and flare wider. If you aspire to be a gentleman, should you not strive with all your might?

sentences.zh: 雖曰恒人，情不能素盡，故當以遠理勝之，么算除之，豈可不務自異，而取陷庸品乎。

translations.literal: Though it is said ordinary men cannot in feeling always be fully pure, therefore one ought to overcome it with far-reaching principle and remove it with minute reckoning—how can one not strive to make oneself distinct, yet instead take the trap of the mediocre grade?
translations.idiomatic: Though ordinary men cannot always master their feelings, you should overcome them with far-reaching principle and cast off petty calculations. Will you not strive to set yourself apart, rather than fall into the common rut?

sentences.zh: :富厚貧薄，事之懸也。

translations.literal: Wealth and want, thick and thin—these are the extremes of affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Wealth and poverty are the two extremes of fortune.

sentences.zh: 以富厚之身，親貧薄之人，非可一時同處。

translations.literal: With a wealthy and ample body to draw near to poor and thin persons is not something that can be shared in one time and place.
translations.idiomatic: The wealthy and the poor cannot long dwell together as equals.

sentences.zh: 然昔有守之無怨，安之不悶者，蓋有理存焉。

translations.literal: Yet in the past there were those who kept to it without resentment and were at ease without vexation—surely principle was present in this.
translations.idiomatic: Yet in old times some kept their station without resentment and lived at ease without distress—there was reason in it.

sentences.zh: 夫既有富厚，必有貧薄，豈其證然，時乃天道。

translations.literal: Since there is wealth and thickness, there must be poverty and thinness—is this not evident proof? It is the season's way of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Where wealth exists, poverty must exist as well—is this not plain? It is Heaven's way in its season.

sentences.zh: 若人皆厚富，是理無貧薄。

translations.literal: If all men were thickly wealthy, then in principle there would be no poverty and thinness.
translations.idiomatic: If all men were rich, then by principle there would be no poor.

sentences.zh: 然乎﹖必不然也。

translations.literal: Is it so? It certainly is not.
translations.idiomatic: Is that so? Certainly not.

sentences.zh: 若謂富厚在我，則宜貧薄在人。

translations.literal: If one says wealth and thickness are in oneself, then poverty and thinness ought to be in others.
translations.idiomatic: If you say wealth belongs to you, then poverty ought to belong to others.

sentences.zh: 可乎﹖又不可矣。

translations.literal: Can it be? Again it cannot.
translations.idiomatic: Can that be? Again, it cannot.

sentences.zh: 道在不然，義在不可，而橫意去就，謬生希幸，以為未達至分。

translations.literal: The Way lies in what is not so; righteousness lies in what cannot be—yet with willful coming and going, wrongly born hope and fortune, one thinks one has not reached the ultimate allotment.
translations.idiomatic: The Way lies in what is not so; right conduct lies in what cannot be—yet men willfully come and go, clutching false hopes, thinking they have not grasped their proper lot.

sentences.zh: :蠶溫農飽，民生之本，躬稼難就，止以僕役為資，當施其情願，庀其衣食，定其當治，遞其優劇，出之休饗，後之捶責，雖有勸恤之勤，而無霑曝之苦。

translations.literal: Silkworms warm and farmers full—the root of the people's life. Personal plowing is hard to accomplish; one stops at using servants as resource. One ought to apply their feelings and wishes, provide their food and clothing, fix what they should manage, rotate light and heavy tasks, give them rest and feasting, put off beating and punishment—though there is the diligence of urging and pity, there is none of the suffering of exposure to sun and rain.
translations.idiomatic: Silkworms and plowing are the root of livelihood. Since you cannot farm with your own hands, you rely on servants: grant their wishes, supply food and clothing, assign proper duties, rotate light and heavy work, give them rest and refreshment, and defer beatings. Urge and comfort them, but do not expose them to sun and rain without need.

sentences.zh: :務前公稅，以遠吏讓，無急傍費，以息流議，量時發斂，視歲穰儉，省贍以奉己，損散以及人，此用天之善，御生之得也。

translations.literal: Attend first to public taxes to keep clerks' blame far off; have no urgent side expenses to quiet floating criticism; measure the time for levying and gathering, regard the year's abundance or scarcity; economize support to maintain oneself and reduce dispersal to reach others—this is using Heaven's goodness and obtaining mastery of life.
translations.idiomatic: Pay public taxes first to keep officials at bay; avoid rash side expenses to silence gossip; levy and gather according to the season, watching whether the year is rich or lean; spare enough for yourself and share what you can—this is using Heaven's bounty and mastering how to live.

sentences.zh: :率下多方，見情為上；

translations.literal: In leading subordinates use many methods; making feeling visible is supreme;
translations.idiomatic: In leading those below, use many methods; let them see your true feeling—

sentences.zh: 立長多術，晦明為懿。

translations.literal: in establishing elders use many arts; hiding and revealing is excellence.
translations.idiomatic: in appointing overseers use many arts; to show and to conceal is excellence.

sentences.zh: 雖及僕妾，情見則事通；

translations.literal: Even reaching servants and concubines, when feeling is seen affairs are penetrated;
translations.idiomatic: Even with servants and concubines, when feeling is seen affairs run clear;

sentences.zh: 雖在畎畝，明晦則功博。

translations.literal: even in field and furrow, when bright and dark are used achievement is broad.
translations.idiomatic: even in the fields, when you show and conceal your purpose, work spreads wide.

sentences.zh: 若奪其常然，役其煩務，使威烈雷霆，猶不禁其欲；

translations.literal: If one seizes their normal course and drives them in troublesome duties, making authority fierce as thunder, still one cannot forbid their desires;
translations.idiomatic: If you seize their normal ways and drive them with endless tasks, though your authority be thunder, you still cannot curb their desires;

sentences.zh: 雖棄其大用，窮其細瑕，或明灼日月，將不勝其邪。

translations.literal: though one abandons their great usefulness and exhausts their minute flaws, or makes brightness blaze like sun and moon, one will not overcome their perversity.
translations.idiomatic: though you discard their great usefulness and hunt their petty faults, though your clarity blaze like sun and moon, you will not master their waywardness.

sentences.zh: 故曰：「孱焉則差，的焉則闇。」

translations.literal: Therefore it is said: "When weak, then error; when pointed, then darkness."
translations.idiomatic: Hence the saying: "Too weak, and you err; too sharp, and you blind."

sentences.zh: 是以禮道尚優，法意從刻。

translations.literal: Therefore ritual's Way esteems leniency; law's intent follows severity.
translations.idiomatic: Therefore ritual esteems leniency, while law inclines to severity.

sentences.zh: 優則人自為厚，刻則物相為薄。

translations.literal: Leniency then makes men themselves thick; severity then makes things mutually thin.
translations.idiomatic: With leniency men grow generous; with severity things grow mean.

sentences.zh: 耕收誠鄙，此用不忒，所謂野陋而不以居心也。

translations.literal: Plowing and harvest are truly base; this use does not err—what is called rustic and coarse yet not taken as the dwelling of the heart.
translations.idiomatic: Farming is humble work, yet rightly used it does not fail—what is called rustic should not fill the heart.

sentences.zh: :含生之氓，同祖一氣，等級相傾，遂成差品，遂使業習移其天識，世服沒其性靈。

translations.literal: All living folk share one ancestral breath; ranks lean upon one another and thus form graded kinds, so that occupational habit shifts their heaven-given knowing and worldly garb drowns their native spirit.
translations.idiomatic: All who live share one breath of life; ranks press upon one another and form degrees, until habit shifts native understanding and worldly custom drowns the inborn spirit.

sentences.zh: 至夫願欲情嗜，宜無間殊，或役人而養給，然是非大意，不可侮也。

translations.literal: As for wishes, desires, feelings, and cravings—there ought to be no difference in kind. Some employ others to feed and supply themselves, yet this is not the great principle and must not be despised.
translations.idiomatic: Wishes and cravings ought not to differ in kind between men. Some employ others to feed themselves—yet this is no small matter and must not be treated lightly.

sentences.zh: 隅奧有竈，齊侯蔑寒，犬馬有秩，管、燕輕饑。

translations.literal: In corner and recess there are stoves; the Marquis of Qi scorned cold; dogs and horses have order; Guan and Yan made light of hunger.
translations.idiomatic: Even in a corner there is a stove; Duke Huan of Qi scorned the cold; dogs and horses have their stations; Guan Zhong and Yan Ying thought little of hunger.

sentences.zh: 若能服溫厚而知穿弊之苦，明周之德；

translations.literal: If one can submit to warmth and thickness and know the suffering of worn rags, one understands the virtue of Zhou;
translations.idiomatic: If you can embrace warmth and plenty and know the pain of threadbare clothes, you understand the virtue of Zhou;

sentences.zh: 厭滋旨而識寡嗛之急，仁恕之功。

translations.literal: if one loathes rich flavors and knows the urgency of scant and frugal fare, this is the achievement of kindness and forbearance.
translations.idiomatic: if you tire of rich fare and know the urgency of plain food, you have achieved kindness and forbearance.

sentences.zh: 豈與夫比肌膚於草石方手足於飛走者同其意用哉。

translations.literal: How could this be the same intent and use as those who compare skin and flesh to grass and stone, or square hands and feet to flying and running beasts?
translations.idiomatic: How can that share the intent of those who compare flesh to grass and stone, or treat hands and feet like beasts' limbs?

sentences.zh: 罰慎其濫，惠戒其偏。

translations.literal: In punishment be wary of excess; in favor be warned against partiality.
translations.idiomatic: In punishment guard against excess; in kindness guard against partiality.

sentences.zh: 罰濫則無以為罰，惠偏則不如無惠。

translations.literal: When punishment is excessive there is no longer punishment; when favor is partial it is better to have no favor.
translations.idiomatic: When punishment runs wild it ceases to be punishment; when kindness is partial it is better to show none.

sentences.zh: 雖爾眇末，猶扁庸保之上，事思反己，動類念物，則其情得，而人心塞矣。

translations.literal: Though you are minute and slight, you still stand above the common hired guard; in affairs think of turning back upon yourself, in movement constantly recall things—then their feeling is obtained and men's hearts are filled.
translations.idiomatic: Though you are slight, you still stand above the hired guard; in affairs turn back upon yourself, in action remember others' lot—then feeling is met and hearts are won.

sentences.zh: :抃博蒲塞，會眾之事，諧調哂謔，適坐之方，然失敬致侮，皆此之由。

translations.literal: Hand-clapping, gambling, and dice are affairs of gathering crowds; harmonious tuning, smiling, and jesting are methods fit for sitting—but loss of respect brings insult, and all these arise from this.
translations.idiomatic: Hand-clapping games and dice are crowd affairs; banter and jest suit a seated gathering—yet loss of respect breeds insult, and all of this springs from such sport.

sentences.zh: 方其剋瞻，彌喪端儼，況遭非鄙，慮將醜折。

translations.literal: Just when one overcomes and gazes, one loses ever more upright dignity; how much more when meeting with what is not base—one fears disgraceful breaking.
translations.idiomatic: At the moment of triumph you lose your dignity all the more; if you meet with vulgar company, you fear a shameful fall.

sentences.zh: 豈若拒其容而簡其事，靜其氣而遠其意，使言必諍厭，賓友清耳，笑不傾撫，左右悅目。

translations.literal: How much better to refuse their manner and simplify their affairs, calm their spirit and keep their intent far off—so that words must be earnest and disliked, guests and friends have clear ears, laughter does not lean and stroke, and those left and right please the eye.
translations.idiomatic: Better to refuse their ways and simplify their affairs, calm your temper and keep their intent at bay—so speech stays earnest, guests hear clearly, laughter does not run wild, and those about you are pleased.

sentences.zh: 非鄙無因而生，侵侮何從而入，此亦持德之管籥，爾其謹哉。

translations.literal: What is not base has no cause to arise; invasion and insult have no way to enter—this too is the key to holding virtue. Be careful of it.
translations.idiomatic: Vulgarity will find no opening; insult will find no entry—this too is the key to holding virtue. Take heed.

sentences.zh: :嫌惑疑心，誠亦難分，豈唯厚貌蔽智之明，深情怯剛之斷而已哉。

translations.literal: Suspicion, delusion, and doubting heart are truly hard to separate—is it only the clarity of thick appearance hiding wisdom, or the judgment of deep feeling fearing hardness?
translations.idiomatic: Suspicion and doubting hearts are hard to tell apart—is it only the wise mask of a thick face, or the timid judgment of deep feeling?

sentences.zh: 必使猜怨愚賢，則嚬笑入戾，期變犬馬，則步顧成妖。

translations.literal: If one must make suspicion and resentment confuse fool and sage, then a frown or smile enters perversity; if one expects change in dogs and horses, then step and glance become portents.
translations.idiomatic: Force suspicion to confuse fool and sage, and a smile becomes perverse; expect dogs and horses to change nature, and every step becomes an omen.

sentences.zh: 況動容竊斧，束裝濫金，又何足論。

translations.literal: How much more when bearing changes like stealing an axe, or bundling luggage and flooding with gold—what is there worth discussing?
translations.idiomatic: How much less when a changed expression seems like the axe-stealer's tale, or packed luggage like Ying's gold—what is worth discussing then?

sentences.zh: 是以前王作典，明慎議獄，而僭濫易意；

translations.literal: Therefore former kings made canons, clearly and cautiously deliberating cases, yet usurpation and excess change intent;
translations.idiomatic: Hence former kings made law and judged cases with care, yet presumption and excess still twist judgment;

sentences.zh: 朱公論璧，光澤相如，而倍薄異價。

translations.literal: Duke Zhu discussed a jade disk: luster and sheen were alike, yet twice over it was thin and the price differed.
translations.idiomatic: Duke Zhu of Yue appraised a jade disk whose luster seemed the same, yet it was twice as thin and fetched a different price.

sentences.zh: 此言雖大，可以戒小。

translations.literal: Though this saying is great, it can warn in small matters.
translations.idiomatic: Though this lesson is drawn from great affairs, it can warn you in small ones.

sentences.zh: :遊道雖廣，交義為長。

translations.literal: Though the way of wandering is broad, the righteousness of friendship is what lasts.
translations.idiomatic: Though the ways of society are many, the bond of friendship is what endures.

sentences.zh: 得在可久，失在輕絕。

translations.literal: Gaining lies in what can last long; losing lies in lightly breaking off.
translations.idiomatic: Success lies in what can endure; failure lies in breaking off lightly.

sentences.zh: 久由相敬，絕由相狎。

translations.literal: Longevity comes from mutual respect; breaking comes from mutual familiarity.
translations.idiomatic: Endurance comes from mutual respect; rupture comes from undue familiarity.

sentences.zh: 愛之勿勞，當扶其正性，忠而勿誨，必藏其枉情。

translations.literal: In loving, do not toil them; one should support their upright nature. In loyalty, do not instruct them; one must conceal their crooked feeling.
translations.idiomatic: In love, do not wear them down—uphold their upright nature. In loyalty, do not preach at them—hide their crooked impulses.

sentences.zh: 輔以藝業，會以文辭，使親不可褻，疏不可間，每存大德，無挾小怨。

translations.literal: Assist with arts and crafts, meet with literary expression, so that the intimate cannot be profaned and the distant cannot be divided; always keep great virtue and do not carry small resentments.
translations.idiomatic: Support them with craft and learning, meet them in letters, so intimacy is not profaned and distance is not wedged apart; keep to great virtue and do not nurse small grudges.

sentences.zh: 率此往也，足以相終。

translations.literal: Leading with this going forward is enough to see each other to the end.
translations.idiomatic: Live by this, and friendship can last to the end.

sentences.zh: :酒酌之設，可樂而不可嗜，嗜而非病者希，病而遂眚者幾。

translations.literal: The setting out of wine and cups may give joy but must not be addicted to; those addicted yet not ill are few, and those ill and then reaching fault are scarce.
translations.idiomatic: Wine may delight but must not be craved; few who crave it escape harm, and few who are harmed escape disgrace.

sentences.zh: 既眚既病，將蔑其正。

translations.literal: Once faulted and ill, one will slight one's rectitude.
translations.idiomatic: Once shamed and sick, you will slight your proper self.

sentences.zh: 若存其正性，紓其妄發，其唯善戒乎。

translations.literal: If one preserves upright nature and loosens reckless outburst, is it not only through good warning?
translations.idiomatic: If you keep your upright nature and restrain reckless excess, can it be done except by good self-warning?

sentences.zh: 聲樂之會，可簡而不可違，違而不背者鮮矣，背而非弊者反矣。

translations.literal: Gatherings of sound and music may be simplified but must not be violated; those who violate yet do not turn away are few, and those who turn away yet are not harmed are the opposite case.
translations.idiomatic: Music and song may be kept simple but not cast aside; few who cast them aside avoid excess, and few who go to excess avoid harm.

sentences.zh: 既弊既背，將受其毀。

translations.literal: Once harmed and turned away, one will receive its ruin.
translations.idiomatic: Once harmed and turned aside, you will suffer ruin.

sentences.zh: 必能通其礙而節其流，意可為和中矣。

translations.literal: One must be able to penetrate its obstruction and regulate its flow—then intent can become harmonizing centrality.
translations.idiomatic: You must clear its blockages and regulate its flow—then your mind can find true balance.

sentences.zh: :善施者豈唯發自人心，乃出天則。

translations.literal: Those good at giving—does it issue only from the human heart? It also comes from Heaven's rule.
translations.idiomatic: True generosity does not spring from the heart alone—it follows Heaven's rule.

sentences.zh: 與不待積，取無謀實，並散千金，誠不可能。

translations.literal: Giving does not wait on accumulation; taking has no plan for substance; to scatter a thousand gold together is truly impossible.
translations.idiomatic: Giving does not wait on hoarding; taking needs no grand scheme; to scatter a thousand gold at once is truly impossible.

sentences.zh: 贍人之急，雖乏必先，使施如王丹，受如杜林，亦可與言交矣。

translations.literal: Relieving others' urgency, though oneself is lacking yet putting them first—if giving is like Wang Dan and receiving like Du Lin, one may also speak of friendship with them.
translations.idiomatic: Relieve others' urgent need, though you yourself are poor—give as Wang Dan gave, receive as Du Lin received, and you may speak of true friendship.

sentences.zh: :浮華怪飾，滅質之具；

translations.literal: Floating splendor and strange adornment are instruments that extinguish substance;
translations.idiomatic: Gaudy ornament and strange dress are tools that destroy substance;

sentences.zh: 奇服麗食，棄素之方。

translations.literal: strange garments and beautiful food are ways of abandoning simplicity.
translations.idiomatic: curious clothes and rich food are ways of abandoning simplicity.

sentences.zh: 動人勸慕，傾人顧盻，可以遠識奪，難用近欲從。

translations.literal: They stir men and urge emulation, overturn men's glances and looks—one can with far-reaching understanding seize them, but it is hard to use near desire to follow them.
translations.idiomatic: They stir men to envy and turn every gaze—far sight may master them, but near desire cannot.

sentences.zh: 若覩其淫怪，知生之無心，為見奇麗，能致諸非務，則不抑自貴，不禁自止。

translations.literal: If one sees their excess and strangeness and knows that life has no [fixed] heart, or for the sake of seeing the strange and beautiful can bring about all non-essential affairs, then without suppressing one esteems oneself, without forbidding one stops oneself.
translations.idiomatic: If you see their excess and know that life has no fixed heart, or chase strange beauty into every idle affair, you will prize yourself without restraint and never stop of your own accord.

sentences.zh: :夫數相者，必有之徵，既聞之術人，又驗之吾身，理可得而論也。

translations.literal: As for those who count and physiognomize, there are sure signs; having heard it from practitioners of arts and having tested it in my own person, principle may be obtained and discussed.
translations.idiomatic: Those who read fate by numbers find sure signs—I have heard it from masters of the art and tested it in my own life; the principle can be reasoned out.

sentences.zh: 人者兆氣二德，禀體五常。

translations.literal: Man is portent-breath and two virtues, receiving in body the five constants.
translations.idiomatic: Man is shaped by portent and breath, by two virtues, and receives in his body the five constants.

sentences.zh: 二德有奇偶，五常有勝殺，及其為人，寧無叶沴。

translations.literal: The two virtues have odd and even; the five constants have overcoming and killing—when it comes to becoming a person, how could there be none that harmonize or clash?
translations.idiomatic: The two virtues have their odd and even; the five constants overcome and restrain one another—when a man is formed, how can there be no harmony or clash?

sentences.zh: 亦猶生有好醜，死有夭壽，人皆知其懸天；

translations.literal: It is also like life having beauty and ugliness, death having early and long span—all men know these hang from Heaven;
translations.idiomatic: As life has beauty and ugliness, death has early end and long span—all know these hang from Heaven;

sentences.zh: 至於丁年乖遇，中身迂合者，豈可易地哉。

translations.literal: as for strong years meeting perverse fortune, or mid-life encountering crooked fit—can these be exchanged for another place?
translations.idiomatic: but as for ill fortune in one's prime or crooked chances in mid-life—can these be swapped for another's lot?

sentences.zh: 是以君子道命愈難，識道愈堅。

translations.literal: Therefore the gentleman, the more difficult his allotted Way, the firmer his knowing of the Way.
translations.idiomatic: Therefore the more difficult a gentleman's fate, the firmer his grasp of the Way.

sentences.zh: :古人恥以身為溪壑者，屏欲之謂也。

translations.literal: The ancients were ashamed to make their persons into ravines and gullies—this is called screening off desire.
translations.idiomatic: The ancients were ashamed to turn themselves into ravines of greed—this is what screening off desire means.

sentences.zh: 欲者，性之煩濁，氣之蒿蒸，故其為害，則燻心智，耗真情，傷人和，犯天性。

translations.literal: Desire is the turbid annoyance of nature and the muggy steaming of breath; therefore its harm is to smoke the mind's knowing, exhaust true feeling, injure human harmony, and violate heaven's nature.
translations.idiomatic: Desire is nature's turbid vexation and breath's steaming heat; its harm is to cloud the mind, drain true feeling, wound human harmony, and violate heaven's nature.

sentences.zh: 雖生必有之，而生之德，猶火含煙而煙妨火，桂懷蠹而蠹殘桂，然則火勝則煙滅，蠹壯則桂折。

translations.literal: Though life must have it, life's virtue is like fire containing smoke yet smoke hindering fire, or cassia harboring borers yet borers ruining cassia—then if fire prevails smoke is extinguished; if borers grow strong cassia is broken.
translations.idiomatic: Life must have desire, yet life's virtue is like fire that holds smoke yet is choked by it, like cassia that harbors borers yet is ruined by them—if fire prevails, smoke dies; if borers thrive, cassia breaks.

sentences.zh: 故性明者欲簡，嗜繁者氣惛，去明即惛，難以生矣。

translations.literal: Therefore those whose nature is bright simplify desire; those who crave the complex have breath benighted—remove brightness and one is benighted; it is hard to live.
translations.idiomatic: Those of bright nature simplify desire; those who crave complexity darken their breath—lose brightness and you darken; it is hard to live.

sentences.zh: 是以中外羣聖，建言所黜，儒道眾智，發論是除。

translations.literal: Therefore sages within and without, in establishing words, dismiss it; the many wisdoms of Confucian and Daoist ways, in issuing discourse, remove it.
translations.idiomatic: Hence sages within and without, in their teachings, cast it aside; Confucians and Daoists, in their doctrines, seek to remove it.

sentences.zh: 然有之者不患誤深，故藥之者恒苦術淺，所以毀道多而於義寡。

translations.literal: Yet those who have it do not fear error going deep; therefore those who would medicate it always suffer shallow technique—hence those who ruin the Way are many while those who hit righteousness are few.
translations.idiomatic: Yet those who harbor desire do not fear falling deep; those who would cure it always find their art too shallow—hence many ruin the Way while few reach righteousness.

sentences.zh: 頓盡誠難，每指可易，能易每指，亦明之末。

translations.literal: To exhaust it at once is truly hard; each pointer can be changed—if one can change each pointer, that too is the end of brightness.
translations.idiomatic: To end it all at once is hard; each impulse can be turned—if you can turn each impulse, you have reached the limit of clarity.

sentences.zh: :廉嗜之性不同，故畏慕之情或異，從事於人者，無一人我之心，不以己之所善謀人，為有明矣。

translations.literal: Frugal craving and nature differ, so feelings of fear and admiration may differ. Those who undertake affairs with others have no heart of self and other; they do not use what they themselves approve to plan for others—this is having clarity.
translations.idiomatic: Men differ in frugality and craving, so fear and admiration differ too. Those who serve others should have no heart of self versus other, and should not impose their own tastes on others—that is clarity.

sentences.zh: 不以人之所務失我，能有守矣。

translations.literal: Not letting what others pursue cause loss to oneself—this is being able to keep guard.
translations.idiomatic: Do not let others' pursuits unsettle you—that is keeping your ground.

sentences.zh: 己所謂然，而彼定不然，弈棊之蔽；

translations.literal: What I call right, yet they surely call not right—this is the blindness of playing go;
translations.idiomatic: What I call right, they surely call wrong—the blindness of the chess player;

sentences.zh: 悅彼之可，而忘我不可，學嚬之蔽。

translations.literal: delighting in what they can do and forgetting what I cannot—this is the blindness of imitating a frown.
translations.idiomatic: delighting in what others can do and forgetting what I cannot—the blindness of mimicking a frown.

sentences.zh: 將求去蔽者，念通怍介而已。

translations.literal: Those who would seek to remove blindness need only think through to shame and boundary.
translations.idiomatic: To remove such blindness, think through to shame and proper bounds.

sentences.zh: :流言謗議，有道所不免，況在闕薄，難用算防。

translations.literal: Floating words and slanderous discussion are what those with the Way cannot avoid; how much more in deficiency and thinness, where it is hard to use reckoning to guard against them.
translations.idiomatic: Rumor and slander are what no man of the Way can wholly escape; how much more for the deficient and slight, where calculation cannot guard against them.

sentences.zh: 接應之方，言必出己。

translations.literal: The method of receiving and responding: words must come from oneself.
translations.idiomatic: In receiving and responding, let your words come from yourself.

sentences.zh: 或信不素積，嫌間所襲，或性不和物，尤怨所聚，有一于此，何處逃毀。

translations.literal: Perhaps trust not long accumulated and suspicion's gap assaults; perhaps nature not in harmony with things and resentment gathers—have one of these, where can one escape ruin?
translations.idiomatic: Perhaps trust was never built and suspicion strikes; perhaps your nature clashes with things and resentment gathers—with any of these, where can ruin be escaped?

sentences.zh: 苟能反悔在我，而無責於人，必有達鑒，昭其情遠，識迹其事。

translations.literal: If one can turn back reflection upon oneself and not blame others, there will surely be penetrating insight that makes feeling clear and distant and knows traces of affairs.
translations.idiomatic: If you can turn reflection upon yourself and blame no other, penetrating insight will clarify your feeling from afar and read the traces of events.

sentences.zh: 日省吾躬，月料吾志，寬默以居，潔靜以期，神道必在，何恤人言。

translations.literal: Daily examine my person, monthly measure my will; dwell in broad silence, expect in pure stillness—the spirit's Way must be present; why worry over men's words?
translations.idiomatic: Examine yourself daily, measure your will monthly; dwell in broad silence and pure stillness—the spirit's Way will be with you; why fear what men say?

sentences.zh: :喭曰，富則盛，貧則病矣。

translations.literal: A proverb says: with wealth one flourishes; with poverty one is afflicted.
translations.idiomatic: A proverb says: wealth brings flourishing; poverty brings affliction.

sentences.zh: 貧之病也，不唯形色粗黶，或亦神心沮廢；

translations.literal: Poverty's affliction is not only coarse form and dark complexion; sometimes spirit and heart are discouraged and ruined;
translations.idiomatic: Poverty afflicts not only the coarse body and darkened face; sometimes spirit and heart are broken;

sentences.zh: 豈但交友疎棄，必有家人誚讓。

translations.literal: how much less only friends growing distant and abandoning—there must also be family reproach and blame.
translations.idiomatic: friends grow distant, and family reproach is sure to follow.

sentences.zh: 非廉深識遠者，何能不移其植。

translations.literal: Unless one is frugal, deep in knowing, and far in sight, how can one not shift one's planting?
translations.idiomatic: Unless you are frugal, deep-sighted, and far-seeing, how can you keep your footing unchanged?

sentences.zh: 故欲蠲憂患，莫若懷古。

translations.literal: Therefore if one wishes to remove worry and calamity, nothing is like cherishing antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: To remove worry and harm, nothing surpasses cherishing antiquity.

sentences.zh: 懷古之志，當自同古人，見通則憂淺，意遠則怨浮，昔有琴歌於編蓬之中者，用此道也。

translations.literal: The will of cherishing antiquity ought to make oneself the same as the ancients; when seeing is penetrating, worry is shallow; when intent is far, resentment floats lightly. In the past there was one who played zither and sang amid woven rushes—he used this Way.
translations.idiomatic: The will to cherish antiquity makes you one with the ancients; broad sight makes worry shallow, far intent makes resentment light. Once a man played zither and sang in a hut of woven rushes—he used this Way.

sentences.zh: :夫信不逆彰，義必幽隱，交賴相盡，明有相照。

translations.literal: Trust does not go against what is manifest; righteousness must be hidden and concealed. Friendship relies on mutual exhaustion; brightness has mutual illumination.
translations.idiomatic: Trust does not contradict what is plain; righteousness dwells in what is hidden. Friendship depends on giving all; clarity shines upon one another.

sentences.zh: 一面見旨，則情固丘岳，一言中志，則意入淵泉。

translations.literal: On one side seeing the intent, then feeling is firm as hills and peaks; one word hitting the will, then thought enters deep springs.
translations.idiomatic: See the intent once face to face, and feeling stands firm as mountains; one word strikes the mark, and thought sinks to the deep spring.

sentences.zh: 以此事上，水火可蹈，以此託友，金石可弊，豈待充其榮實，乃將議報，厚之篚筐，然後圖終。

translations.literal: With this to serve superiors, fire and water can be trodden; with this to entrust friendship, metal and stone can be worn away. Must one wait to fill their glory and substance before discussing repayment, heaping baskets and then planning the end?
translations.idiomatic: Serve your lord thus and you may tread fire and water; entrust friendship thus and metal and stone may wear away. Must you wait to heap glory and fruit before speaking of repayment, fill baskets and only then plan the end?

sentences.zh: 如或與立，茂思無忽。

translations.literal: If perhaps you stand with another, in lush thought do not neglect.
translations.idiomatic: If you stand with another, in generous thought do not neglect him.

sentences.zh: :祿利者受之易，易則人之所榮；

translations.literal: Salary and profit are received easily; what is easy is what men honor;
translations.idiomatic: Salary and profit are easily received; what is easy men honor;

sentences.zh: 蠶穡者就之艱，艱則物之所鄙。

translations.literal: silkworms and harvest are approached with hardship; what is hard is what things despise.
translations.idiomatic: silkworms and the plow are hard to pursue; what is hard things despise.

sentences.zh: 艱易既有勤倦之情，榮鄙又間向背之意，此二塗所為反也。

translations.literal: Hard and easy already have feelings of diligence and weariness; honor and baseness also have between them inclinations of turning toward and turning away—these two paths act in opposition.
translations.idiomatic: Hard and easy bring diligence or weariness; honor and baseness turn men toward or away—these two paths run counter.

sentences.zh: 以勞定國，以功施人，則役徒屬而擅豐麗；

translations.literal: With toil settling the state and merit bestowing on men, one drives subordinates and monopolizes abundance and splendor;
translations.idiomatic: Settle the state by toil and bestow merit on men, and you drive subordinates while hoarding splendor;

sentences.zh: 自埋於民，自事其生，則督妻子而趨耕織。

translations.literal: bury oneself among the people and attend to one's own living, then one urges wife and children to hurry to plowing and weaving.
translations.idiomatic: bury yourself among the people and tend your own life, and you urge wife and children to plow and weave.

sentences.zh: 必使陵侮不作，懸企不萌，所謂賢鄙處宜，華野同泰。

translations.literal: One must make overbearing insult not arise and suspended longing not sprout—what is called worthy and base each in their place, splendor and wildness equally at peace.
translations.idiomatic: See that arrogance does not arise and envy does not sprout—let worthy and base each keep their place, court and field alike at peace.

sentences.zh: :人以有惜為質，非假嚴刑；

translations.literal: Men take having cherishing care as their substance; it does not borrow severe punishment;
translations.idiomatic: Men's substance lies in cherishing what they have; it does not depend on harsh punishment;

sentences.zh: 有恒為德，不慕厚貴。

translations.literal: having constancy is virtue; not admiring thick wealth and honor.
translations.idiomatic: constancy is virtue; do not crave thick wealth and rank.

sentences.zh: 有惜者，以理葬；

translations.literal: Those who cherish care bury with principle;
translations.idiomatic: Those who cherish what they have bury with reason;

sentences.zh: 有恒者，與物終。

translations.literal: those with constancy end with things.
translations.idiomatic: those with constancy see things through to the end.

sentences.zh: 世有位去則情盡，斯無惜矣。

translations.literal: In the world, when rank departs feeling is exhausted—then there is no cherishing.
translations.idiomatic: In the world, when office departs, feeling fades—then there is no true cherishing.

sentences.zh: 又有務謝則心移，斯不恒矣。

translations.literal: Again, when affairs decline the heart shifts—then there is no constancy.
translations.idiomatic: When affairs decline the heart shifts—then there is no constancy.

sentences.zh: 又非徒若此而已，或見人休事，則懃蘄結納，及聞否論，則處彰離貳，附會以從風，隱竊以成釁，朝吐面譽，暮行背毀，昔同稽款，今猶叛戾，斯為甚矣。

translations.literal: Again it is not only thus and no more—some see others' affairs prosper and then diligently seek ties and acceptance; when they hear denial or blame they stand apart in manifest division, attach themselves to follow the wind, conceal theft to make quarrels, praise to the face at dawn and slander behind the back at dusk; once they bowed together in reverence, now they still rebel and depart—this is extreme indeed.
translations.idiomatic: Nor is this the whole of it: some see another prosper and eagerly court him; when they hear he has fallen, they stand aloof in open disloyalty. They trim their sails to every wind, hide malice to breed strife, praise to his face at dawn and slander him at dusk. Men who once bowed together now turn traitor—nothing is worse.

sentences.zh: 又非唯若此而已，或憑人惠訓，藉人成立，與人餘論，依人揚聲，曲存禀仰，甘赴塵軌。

translations.literal: Again it is not only thus—some rely on others' kindness and instruction, borrow others to establish themselves, join in others' spare discourse, depend on others to raise their reputation, bend to preserve deference, and gladly rush onto the dusty track.
translations.idiomatic: And there is more: some lean on another's kindness and teaching, borrow another's standing to make their own, ride on others' gossip, borrow others' voice for fame, bow low in feigned respect, and gladly run the dusty road of servility.

sentences.zh: 衰沒畏遠，忌聞影迹，又蒙蔽其善，毀之無度，心短彼能，私樹己拙，自崇恒輩，罔顧高識，有人至此，實蠹大倫。

translations.literal: When decline comes they fear distance and hate to hear any trace; they veil others' good points and slander without limit, belittle others' ability in the heart, privately plant their own clumsiness, esteem their own constant ilk, disregard lofty understanding—for anyone to reach this point truly gnaws at great human order.
translations.idiomatic: When fortune fades they shun the fallen and hate the slightest rumor of them; they hide others' virtues and slander without measure, resent another's talent, exalt their own mediocrity, honor only their own sort, and scorn the truly wise. Whoever comes to this truly devours the great bonds of human society.

sentences.zh: 每思防避，無通閭伍。

translations.literal: Whenever I think of it I seek to guard and avoid—let none pass through the neighborhood.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I think of such men I seek to keep my distance—let none of them pass through my lane.

sentences.zh: :覩驚異之事，或涉流傳；

translations.literal: When one sees startling and strange matters, one may get involved in spreading them;
translations.idiomatic: When one sees startling or strange things, one may get caught up in spreading them;

sentences.zh: 遭卒迫之變，反思安順。

translations.literal: When one meets sudden and pressing change, one then reflects on peace and compliance.
translations.idiomatic: when sudden crisis strikes, one then turns back to calm and obedience.

sentences.zh: 若異從己發，將尸謗人，迫而又迕，愈使失度。

translations.literal: If the strangeness issues from oneself, one will lay slander on others; pressed and again at odds, one only makes conduct lose measure all the more.
translations.idiomatic: If the wonder springs from oneself, one will lay blame on others; pressed hard and at odds again, conduct loses all proper measure.

sentences.zh: 能夷異如裴楷，處逼如裴遐，可稱深士乎。

translations.literal: To level strangeness as Pei Kai did, to meet pressure as Pei Xia did—can one be called a profound person?
translations.idiomatic: To treat the strange as calmly as Pei Kai, to meet coercion as steadily as Pei Xia—can one be called a man of depth?

sentences.zh: :喜怒者有性所不能無，常起於褊量，而止於弘識。

translations.literal: Joy and anger are what nature cannot be without; they often rise from narrow measure and stop at broad understanding.
translations.idiomatic: Joy and anger are what nature cannot abolish; they usually rise from narrowness and end in magnanimity.

sentences.zh: 然喜過則不重，怒過則不威，能以恬漠為體，寬愉為器，則為美矣。

translations.literal: Yet if joy goes too far one is not weighty; if anger goes too far one is not awe-inspiring—if one can take tranquil indifference as substance and generous pleasure as vessel, that is beautiful.
translations.idiomatic: Yet excess of joy makes one light; excess of anger robs one of dignity. To take calm detachment as one's substance and easy generosity as one's vessel—that is the ideal.

sentences.zh: 大喜蕩心，微抑則定，甚怒煩性，小忍即歇。

translations.literal: Great joy unsettles the heart; a slight restraint and it settles; great anger troubles nature; a little patience and it ceases.
translations.idiomatic: Great joy shakes the heart—a slight check steadies it; great anger harrows the temper—a little patience ends it.

sentences.zh: 故動無愆容，舉無失度，則物將自懸，人將自止。

translations.literal: Therefore if in movement there is no offending bearing and in conduct no lapse of measure, things will suspend themselves and people will stop themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Therefore if your bearing never offends and your conduct never exceeds measure, affairs will right themselves and others will restrain themselves.

sentences.zh: :習之所變亦大矣，豈唯蒸性染身，乃將移智易慮。

translations.literal: What habit changes is also great—not only steaming nature and dyeing the body, but also shifting intelligence and changing counsel.
translations.idiomatic: What habit can change is vast: it does not only steep the nature and stain the body, but can shift the mind and alter one's plans.

sentences.zh: 故曰：「與善人居，如入芷蘭之室，久而不知其芬。」

translations.literal: Hence it is said: "Dwell with good men as if entering a room of angelica and orchids; long therein and you do not know the fragrance."
translations.idiomatic: Hence it is said: "Live among good men as if entering a room of iris and orchid; stay long and you no longer notice the fragrance."

sentences.zh: 與之化矣。

translations.literal: One is transformed by them.
translations.idiomatic: You are transformed by them.

sentences.zh: 「與不善人居，如入鮑魚之肆，久而不知其臭」。

translations.literal: "Dwell with bad men as if entering a salted-fish market; long therein and you do not know the stink."
translations.idiomatic: "Live among bad men as if entering a fishmonger's stall; stay long and you no longer notice the stench."

sentences.zh: 與之變矣。

translations.literal: One is altered by them.
translations.idiomatic: You are altered by them.

sentences.zh: 是以古人慎所與處。

translations.literal: Therefore the ancients were careful whom they associated with.
translations.idiomatic: Therefore the ancients were careful whom they kept company with.

sentences.zh: 唯夫金真玉粹者，乃能盡而不汙爾。

translations.literal: Only those of gold-truth and jade-purity can go to the end yet not be stained.
translations.idiomatic: Only those of gold fidelity and jade purity can go to the end and not be stained.

sentences.zh: 故曰：「丹可滅而不能使無赤，石可毀而不可使無堅。」

translations.literal: Hence it is said: "Cinnabar may be extinguished yet cannot be made to have no red; stone may be destroyed yet cannot be made to have no hardness."
translations.idiomatic: Hence it is said: "Cinnabar may be consumed yet cannot be stripped of redness; stone may be broken yet cannot be stripped of hardness."

sentences.zh: 苟無丹石之性，必慎浸染之由。

translations.literal: If one lacks the nature of cinnabar and stone, one must be careful of the source of steeping dye.
translations.idiomatic: If you lack the nature of cinnabar and stone, you must guard against what steeps and stains you.

sentences.zh: 能以懷道為念，必存從理之心。

translations.literal: If one can take cherishing the Way as thought, one must keep a heart of following principle.
translations.idiomatic: If you can make cherishing the Way your constant thought, you will keep a heart that follows principle.

sentences.zh: 道可懷而理可從，則不議貧，議所樂爾。

translations.literal: If the Way can be cherished and principle followed, then one does not debate poverty but debates what one delights in.
translations.idiomatic: When the Way can be held and principle followed, one does not argue about poverty but about what brings joy.

sentences.zh: 或云：「貧何由樂﹖」此未求道意。

translations.literal: Some say: "How can poverty be delight?"—this has not yet sought the meaning of the Way.
translations.idiomatic: Some say, "How can the poor be happy?"—that is not yet to have sought the meaning of the Way.

sentences.zh: 道者，瞻富貴同貧賤，理固得而齊。

translations.literal: The Way looks on wealth and honor the same as poverty and baseness; principle by nature can be made equal.
translations.idiomatic: The Way views wealth and honor no differently from poverty and low estate; principle by nature can level them.

sentences.zh: 自我喪之，未為通議，苟議不喪，夫何不樂。

translations.literal: To lose it oneself is not yet thorough discussion; if discussion does not lose it, why would one not rejoice?
translations.idiomatic: To lose the Way through one's own fault is not yet sound reasoning; if reasoning does not lose it, why should one not rejoice?

sentences.zh: :或曰，溫飽之貴，所以榮生，饑寒在躬，空曰從道，取諸其身，將非篤論，此又通理所用。

translations.literal: Some say: the value of warmth and fullness is what honors life; hunger and cold on the person, yet empty talk of following the Way—taking it from one's own body, will that not be sincere discussion? This too is what thorough principle uses.
translations.idiomatic: Some object that warmth and a full belly are what dignify life; with hunger and cold upon you, to speak emptily of following the Way and judge it by your own body—is that not earnest argument? This too is a point thorough principle must answer.

sentences.zh: 凡養生之具，豈間定實，或以膏腴夭性，有以菽藿登年。

translations.literal: All instruments for nourishing life—how could they fix reality? Some with rich fare shorten nature; some with beans and coarse greens reach long years.
translations.idiomatic: All means of sustaining life—how could they fix one truth? Rich food sometimes shortens life; beans and coarse greens sometimes carry one to old age.

sentences.zh: 中散云，所足在內，不由於外。

translations.literal: The Master of Scatter said: what suffices is within, not from without.
translations.idiomatic: Ji Kang said that what truly suffices lies within, not in outward things.

sentences.zh: 是以稱體而食，貧歲愈嗛；

translations.literal: Therefore eat according to the body—in poor years all the more sparing;
translations.idiomatic: Therefore eat according to your body's need—in lean years all the more frugal;

sentences.zh: 量腹而炊，豐家餘飡。

translations.literal: cook according to the belly—in rich households leftover meals.
